eras.name: Foundations (birth of AI)
eras.start_event: McCulloch & Pitts publish 'A logical calculus of the ideas immanent in nervous activity' (1943), the first formal model of a neural network.
eras.end_event: Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence (summer 1956), proposed in a document dated 31 Aug 1955 that introduced the term 'artificial intelligence'.
eras.justification: 1943 is the standard start because the McCulloch–Pitts neuron is the first mathematical model of networked computation in the brain; Turing's 1950 paper supplies the test framing. 1956 closes the era because Dartmouth is the conventional founding of AI as a named research field.
eras.quant_marker: Epoch's notable set starts with Shannon's Theseus maze mouse (1950, ~40 FLOP); Rosenblatt's Mark I Perceptron (1957) is ~6.95×10^5 FLOP.
eras.note: [12 Nov verification] Marker verified in Epoch CSV. Boundary years are historiographical conventions, not measured breaks. Primary documents not opened in this session (web fetch blocked); details confirmed via search summaries.

eras.name: Early optimism (the 'golden years')
eras.start_event: Dartmouth workshop (about 18 Jun–17 Aug 1956 per Solomonoff's notes).
eras.end_event: DARPA cuts back undirected AI research in 1973–74 (e.g. cancelling ~$3M a year of Speech Understanding Research grants at CMU), following the 1969 Mansfield Amendment and the UK Lighthill report (published early 1973).
eras.justification: Era of symbolic programs, the perceptron (1958), ELIZA (1966) and Shakey (late 1960s) and of public predictions of near-term human-level AI. It ends when the two largest funders (DARPA in the US, the Science Research Council in the UK) withdrew support for basic AI research.
eras.note: End date varies by source (1973 for the UK, 1974 for DARPA). Sources do not establish that Lighthill caused the DARPA cuts; treat them as parallel events.

eras.name: First AI winter
eras.end_event: Commercial expert systems arrive: McDermott's R1/XCON paper (AAAI 1980) and deployment at Digital Equipment Corporation (in production by about 1980–81).
eras.justification: Funding scarcity and diminished expectations. 1980 is used as the end because rule-based expert systems began earning money for companies, reviving investment.
eras.quant_marker: No compute series point; Epoch's database is sparse for 1974–1980.
eras.note: '1974–1980' is a convention; some accounts start the winter in 1973 (UK).

eras.name: Expert-systems boom
eras.start_event: R1/XCON at DEC (1980); Japan's Fifth Generation Computer Systems project (ICOT) launched 1982 with a ~¥54 billion ten-year budget.
eras.end_event: Collapse of the market for specialised Lisp machines (1987) as general-purpose workstations and PCs became powerful enough to run the same software.
eras.justification: Commercial and government money flowed into knowledge-based systems and dedicated AI hardware; backpropagation was popularised (Nature, 9 Oct 1986). The era ends with the AI-hardware market collapse.
eras.note: XCON savings are reported as ~$25M a year in most accounts; DEC's $40M claim covered related systems too.

eras.name: Second AI winter
eras.end_event: Convention: early-1990s end of the expert-systems retrenchment and of Japan's FGCS project (ten-year term to 1992); statistical and machine-learning methods move centre-stage.
eras.justification: Funding and corporate interest in 'AI' branding fell. 1993 is a convention used by several histories; there is no single event.
eras.note: JUDGEMENT CALL: Wikipedia's AI-winter article dates the second winter 1987–2000; Holloway's history uses 1987–1993. We use 1993 as requested but the page should say the end date is disputed.

eras.name: Statistical machine learning
eras.end_event: IBM Watson wins Jeopardy! (Feb 2011) and Siri ships (Oct 2011) — the last major milestones before deep learning took over.
eras.justification: Probabilistic and kernel methods, plus game-tree search: Deep Blue (1997), LeNet-5 (1998), the DARPA Grand Challenge (2005), deep belief nets (2006), ImageNet's first challenge (2010). Training compute still roughly followed Moore's law (doubling ~every 20 months before 2010, Sevilla et al. 2022).
eras.note: Some histories end this era at 2009–2010 (pre-ImageNet deep nets) — we keep 2011 so AlexNet (Sep 2012) opens the next one.

eras.name: Deep learning
eras.start_event: AlexNet wins ILSVRC 2012 (results 30 Sep 2012) with 15.3% top-5 error vs 26.2% for the runner-up.
eras.end_event: 'Attention Is All You Need' (arXiv 12 Jun 2017) introduces the Transformer.
eras.justification: GPU-trained deep networks win in vision, speech and games (AlphaGo 2016). Sevilla et al. measure a ~6-month compute doubling time from the early 2010s.
eras.quant_marker: Largest estimated runs rose from ~6×10^17 FLOP (2012) to ~6.6×10^21 FLOP (GNMT, 2016) in Epoch's notable set; AlexNet itself was 4.7×10^17.
eras.note: [12 Nov verification] CORRECTED marker: previously cited AlphaGo Zero at ~3×10^23, which Epoch now puts at 6.5×10^20 (direct training only).

eras.name: Transformers and scale
eras.justification: Pre-trained language models scale by orders of magnitude (BERT 2018, GPT-2 2019, GPT-3 2020, PaLM 2022) while remaining research/developer products.
eras.quant_marker: Transformer 7.4×10^18 FLOP (2017) → PaLM 2.5×10^24 FLOP (2022): ~340,000× in five years (DERIVED: 2.5e24 / 7.4e18).

eras.name: Generative AI goes mainstream
eras.start_event: ChatGPT (30 Nov 2022); UBS estimated 100M monthly users by January 2023.
eras.end_event: OpenAI o1-preview (12 Sep 2024) opens the reasoning-model era; Anthropic's computer use (22 Oct 2024) opens the agent era.
eras.justification: Consumer chatbots, image generators and enterprise pilots; GPT-4 (Mar 2023) sets the frontier. McKinsey's adoption measure jumps from 55% (2023) to 72% (early 2024).
eras.quant_marker: GPT-4 2.1×10^25 FLOP and ~$78M estimated training cost (2023).

eras.name: Reasoning models and agents
eras.justification: Gains come increasingly from post-training and inference-time compute rather than only pre-training scale (Epoch estimates GPT-5 used ~5×10^25 FLOP, less than GPT-4.5). Agents dominate traffic on some platforms: OpenRouter reported 76% of October 2026 tokens from agentic keys.
eras.quant_marker: Largest estimated training run: GPT-6 Astra ~9.4×10^26 FLOP (Sep 2026, Epoch via secondary source); SWE-bench Verified saturated at ~97% (Sep 2026).
eras.note: [12 Nov verification] GPT-6 Astra figure verified in Epoch CSV; GPT-5 is ~6.6e25 in the CSV. [Report AI data: tokens.json#openrouter_agent_token_share; models.json#swe_bench_verified_top]. 'Ongoing' — set end=null in charts.

milestones.title: McCulloch–Pitts neuron
milestones.significance: First mathematical model of a network of simplified neurons computing logical functions.
milestones.source: McCulloch & Pitts, Bulletin of Mathematical Biophysics 5
milestones.note: Paper not opened; confirmed via search summaries.

milestones.title: Turing's 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence'
milestones.significance: Replaces 'Can machines think?' with the imitation game (Turing test).
milestones.quant_hook: Turing predicted that in about 50 years machines with ~10^9 storage would leave an average interrogator no more than a 70% chance of a correct identification after five minutes.
milestones.note: 70%/5-minute wording from the paper as widely quoted; the search summary did not show the passage, so MEDIUM.

milestones.title: Dartmouth proposal coins 'artificial intelligence'
milestones.significance: McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon propose a summer study; the document introduces the term.
milestones.quant_hook: Proposed as a '2 month, 10 man study'.
milestones.source: AI Magazine reprint of the proposal
milestones.note: Some sources date the formal submission 2 Sep 1955.

milestones.title: Dartmouth Summer Research Project
milestones.significance: Conventional founding event of AI as a field.
milestones.quant_hook: Ran roughly 18 Jun–17 Aug 1956 (about eight weeks) per Solomonoff's notes; other accounts say six weeks.

milestones.title: Rosenblatt's perceptron unveiled
milestones.significance: First learning machine to attract mass publicity; the US Navy's ONR demonstrated it in July 1958 (a simulation on an IBM 704).
milestones.quant_hook: Mark I Perceptron used a 400-sensor 'retina' and ~1,000 weights; Epoch estimates its training compute at ~6.95×10^5 FLOP.
milestones.source: Rosenblatt, Psychological Review 65(6) 1958; Wikipedia Mark I Perceptron
milestones.note: [12 Nov verification] Compute and parameters verified in Epoch CSV (Epoch dates the Mark I row 1957). Hardware build date given as 1957 or 1960 by different sources.

milestones.title: Shakey the robot (SRI)
milestones.significance: First mobile robot to reason about its own actions; its STRIPS planner became the basis for later automated planners.
milestones.note: Project usually dated 1966–1972; dates not confirmed in this session.

milestones.title: ELIZA
milestones.significance: Weizenbaum's pattern-matching 'therapist' program; first widely known chatbot and first demonstration of people over-attributing understanding to software.
milestones.note: Developed 1964–66 at MIT.

milestones.title: Mansfield Amendment and 'Perceptrons'
milestones.significance: US law pushes DARPA toward mission-oriented research; Minsky & Papert's book highlights single-layer perceptron limits.
milestones.note: Both are commonly cited contributors to the first winter; causation is debated.

milestones.title: Lighthill report
milestones.significance: UK Science Research Council review concludes AI had failed its grand promises; UK funding is sharply curtailed. Debated on BBC TV in June 1973.

milestones.title: DARPA cuts AI funding
milestones.significance: Marks the start of the first AI winter in the US.
milestones.quant_hook: DARPA cancelled ~$3M a year of Speech Understanding Research grants at Carnegie Mellon.

milestones.title: R1/XCON at Digital Equipment Corporation
milestones.significance: First commercially significant expert system; starts the expert-systems boom.
milestones.quant_hook: Most sources put savings at ~$25M a year; by 1986 it had processed 80,000 orders at 95–98% accuracy.
milestones.note: DEC's often-quoted $40M figure covered XCON and related systems.

milestones.title: Japan's Fifth Generation project (ICOT)
milestones.significance: Ten-year MITI programme for logic-programming computers; spurred Western counter-programmes.
milestones.quant_hook: Initial budget ~¥54 billion over ten years; total spending a little under ¥57 billion (~$320M) by the end.
milestones.note: Dollar equivalents vary with the exchange-rate year used; quote yen.

milestones.title: Backpropagation popularised
milestones.significance: Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams show multi-layer networks learn useful internal representations.
milestones.note: Method itself predates it: Linnainmaa (1970), Werbos (1974 thesis), Parker (1985).

milestones.title: Lisp-machine market collapses; NETtalk
milestones.significance: End of dedicated AI hardware boom marks the second AI winter; same year NETtalk shows a neural net learning to pronounce text.
milestones.quant_hook: NETtalk training compute ~2.8×10^10 FLOP (Epoch).

milestones.title: Deep Blue beats Kasparov
milestones.significance: First defeat of a reigning world chess champion by a computer in a match under tournament conditions.
milestones.quant_hook: Won the rematch 3½–2½ (two wins, one loss, three draws); evaluated ~200 million positions per second. Kasparov had won the 1996 match 4–2.

milestones.title: LSTM
milestones.significance: Hochreiter & Schmidhuber's long short-term memory, the recurrent architecture behind most sequence models until the Transformer.
milestones.note: Not re-checked in this session.

milestones.title: LeNet-5
milestones.significance: LeCun et al.'s convolutional network for handwriting recognition, deployed for cheque reading.
milestones.quant_hook: Training compute ~2.8×10^12 FLOP (Epoch, 'Confident').

milestones.title: DARPA Grand Challenge won
milestones.significance: Stanford's Stanley completes a 132-mile desert course autonomously, a year after no vehicle finished.
milestones.quant_hook: 6 h 53 min 58 s; in 2004 the best vehicle managed ~7.4 miles.

milestones.title: Deep belief nets
milestones.significance: Hinton, Osindero & Teh show deep networks can be trained layer by layer, reviving neural-network research.

milestones.title: First ImageNet challenge (ILSVRC)
milestones.significance: Establishes the benchmark that later showcased deep learning.
milestones.quant_hook: Winning top-5 error 28.2% (NEC-UIUC).

milestones.title: IBM Watson wins Jeopardy!
milestones.significance: Open-domain question answering beats the show's two best champions on TV.
milestones.quant_hook: Two-game totals: Watson $77,147; Ken Jennings $24,000; Brad Rutter $21,600.

milestones.title: Siri ships on iPhone 4S
milestones.significance: First voice assistant in mainstream consumer use.
milestones.note: Exact launch day not confirmed in this session.

milestones.title: AlexNet wins ImageNet
milestones.significance: GPU-trained deep convolutional net wins by a wide margin, triggering the deep-learning era.
milestones.quant_hook: Top-5 error 15.3% vs 26.2% for the second-best entry; ~60M parameters; trained on two GTX 580 GPUs; ~4.7×10^17 FLOP (Epoch).
milestones.source: Krizhevsky, Sutskever & Hinton, NIPS 2012; Epoch AI

milestones.title: Google acquires DeepMind
milestones.significance: Big Tech begins buying frontier AI labs.
milestones.quant_hook: Price undisclosed; reported at $400M (Re/code) to more than $500M (The Information).

milestones.title: Generative adversarial networks
milestones.significance: Goodfellow et al. introduce GANs, the main image-generation method until diffusion models.

milestones.title: Sequence-to-sequence learning
milestones.significance: Sutskever, Vinyals & Le show end-to-end neural machine translation with LSTMs.
milestones.quant_hook: Training compute ~5.6×10^19 FLOP (Epoch).
milestones.note: Paper date not re-checked.

milestones.title: ResNet beats human-level ImageNet error
milestones.significance: Residual networks win ILSVRC 2015.
milestones.quant_hook: Top-5 error 3.57%, below the 5.1% single-annotator human estimate.

milestones.title: AlphaGo defeats Lee Sedol
milestones.significance: First defeat of a 9-dan Go professional without handicap, a decade earlier than many expected.
milestones.quant_hook: 4–1 in Seoul, 9–15 Mar 2016; AlphaGo had beaten Fan Hui 5–0 in Oct 2015 (Nature, 27 Jan 2016).

milestones.title: The Transformer
milestones.significance: 'Attention Is All You Need' introduces the architecture behind every frontier language model since.
milestones.quant_hook: 28.4 BLEU on WMT14 English–German; ~7.4×10^18 FLOP training compute (Epoch).

milestones.title: AlphaGo Zero
milestones.significance: Learns Go from self-play alone, without human games; among the first models trained on >10^23 FLOP.
milestones.quant_hook: ~6.5×10^20 FLOP of direct training compute (Epoch, 'Confident'); OpenAI's 2018 figure of ~3.4×10^23 included self-play data generation.
milestones.source: Epoch AI Notable AI Models CSV
milestones.note: [12 Nov verification] CORRECTED hook: was ~3e23 FLOP. Epoch treats AlphaGo Master/Zero as outliers in trend fits.

milestones.title: OpenAI 'AI and Compute'
milestones.significance: First widely cited measurement of exploding training compute.
milestones.quant_hook: More than 300,000× growth from AlexNet to AlphaGo Zero; 3.4-month doubling time (2012–2018).

milestones.title: BERT
milestones.significance: Pre-trained bidirectional Transformer resets most language-understanding benchmarks.
milestones.quant_hook: BERT-Large ~340M parameters; ~2.8×10^20 FLOP (Epoch).

milestones.title: GPT-2 and staged release
milestones.significance: OpenAI withholds the full model at first over misuse concerns, starting the release-norms debate.
milestones.quant_hook: 1.5B parameters; ~1.9×10^21 FLOP (Epoch).
milestones.note: Exact date not re-checked in this session.

milestones.title: GPT-3
milestones.significance: Shows few-shot learning emerges from scale.
milestones.quant_hook: 175B parameters; 3.14×10^23 FLOP; 43.9% on MMLU (few-shot); ~$4.3M estimated training cost (AI Index 2024).

milestones.title: AlphaFold 2 at CASP14
milestones.significance: Effectively solves single-chain protein structure prediction, a 50-year-old problem.
milestones.quant_hook: Median 92.4 GDT across all targets (≈90 is considered competitive with experiment).

milestones.title: PaLM
milestones.significance: Largest dense model of its time; strong reasoning results.
milestones.quant_hook: 540B parameters; ~2.5×10^24 FLOP (Epoch).
milestones.note: Release month from secondary source.

milestones.title: Stable Diffusion released with open weights
milestones.significance: High-quality image generation runs on consumer hardware.

milestones.title: ChatGPT launches

milestones.title: GPT-4

stop_quoting.claim: The term 'artificial intelligence' was coined at the 1956 Dartmouth conference.
stop_quoting.fact: It first appears in the Dartmouth proposal dated 31 August 1955 (McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester, Shannon). The workshop itself ran in summer 1956 — about 18 June to 17 August per Solomonoff's notes, six weeks in other accounts — and attendance varied; the proposal asked for a '2 month, 10 man study'.
stop_quoting.source: AI Magazine reprint of the proposal; Wikipedia (Dartmouth workshop)

stop_quoting.claim: The AI winters were 1974–1980 and 1987–1993.
stop_quoting.fact: These are conventions. UK cuts followed the Lighthill report in 1973; DARPA's cuts came in 1973–74. For the second winter Wikipedia gives 1987–2000 while other histories use 1987–1993. Say 'roughly' and name the defining events (DARPA cuts; Lisp-machine collapse).

stop_quoting.claim: Hinton invented backpropagation in 1986.
stop_quoting.fact: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams popularised it for neural networks (Nature, 9 Oct 1986). The method appeared earlier: Linnainmaa's 1970 master's thesis (reverse-mode differentiation), Werbos's 1974 Harvard thesis, Parker (1985).

stop_quoting.claim: Minsky and Papert's 'Perceptrons' (1969) killed neural-network research and caused the AI winter.
stop_quoting.fact: It was one factor among several. The 1969 Mansfield Amendment redirected DARPA money to mission-oriented work, and the Lighthill report (1973) hit UK funding. Sources do not establish a single cause.

stop_quoting.claim: Deep Blue beat Kasparov in 1996.
stop_quoting.fact: Kasparov won the February 1996 match 4–2 (Deep Blue won one game, on 10 Feb 1996). Deep Blue won the May 1997 rematch 3½–2½, with the decisive game on 11 May 1997.

stop_quoting.claim: A chatbot passed the Turing test in 2014 (Eugene Goostman).
stop_quoting.fact: At a University of Reading event on 7 June 2014, 33% of 30 judges were fooled in five-minute chats by a bot posing as a 13-year-old Ukrainian boy. That clears an organiser-chosen 30% bar, not a standard Turing set: his 1950 paper made a prediction (no more than a 70% chance of correct identification after five minutes by about 2000), not a pass criterion.

stop_quoting.claim: Humans make 5.1% errors on ImageNet, so AI beat humans in 2015.
stop_quoting.fact: 5.1% is one trained annotator (Andrej Karpathy) on a sample of validation images in 2014; two-thirds of his errors came from not knowing the 1,000 classes. ResNet's 3.57% (Dec 2015) beat that single estimate, not 'humans'.

stop_quoting.claim: ChatGPT reached 100 million users in two months — the fastest-growing app ever.
stop_quoting.fact: The 100M figure was a UBS estimate of monthly users in January 2023 from Similarweb web-traffic data, not an OpenAI disclosure; OpenAI's own first 100M figure was weekly users in November 2023. Threads passed 100 million sign-ups in five days in July 2023 — sign-ups, not active users, so the two records are not comparable.

stop_quoting.claim: GPT-4 has 1.76 trillion parameters.
stop_quoting.fact: OpenAI has never disclosed it. 1.76T traces to George Hotz's speculation; Semafor reported ~1T and SemiAnalysis ~1.8T. The mixture-of-experts design is also unconfirmed. Stanford's AI Index 2026 notes frontier labs have stopped reporting parameter counts. Note that even Epoch's database stores 1.8T in its Parameters field, explicitly flagged in its notes as a rumour — do not cite Epoch as confirmation.

stop_quoting.claim: GPT-4 scored in the top 10% on the bar exam.
stop_quoting.fact: OpenAI's percentile compared GPT-4 with February Illinois bar takers, a group skewed towards repeat takers. A 2024 re-evaluation (Artificial Intelligence and Law) found a much lower percentile against first-time or all July takers — Live Science summarised it as not breaking the 70th percentile.

stop_quoting.claim: AI training compute doubles every 3.4 months.
stop_quoting.fact: That was OpenAI's 2018 estimate for 2012–2018. Epoch's longer series gives ~5.7–6 months for the deep-learning era, about 4–5× a year for notable models since 2010 and ~5× a year for frontier language models since 2020. Before 2010 the doubling time was about 20 months.
stop_quoting.source: OpenAI 2018; Sevilla et al. 2022; Epoch AI

stop_quoting.claim: OpenAI's o3 solved 25% of FrontierMath.
stop_quoting.fact: 25.2% was OpenAI's own December 2024 run, probably with more compute or scaffolding. Epoch's independent test of the released o3 in April 2025 found about 10%. OpenAI had funded the benchmark and had access to many problems, which Epoch disclosed only later.

stop_quoting.claim: AlphaGo Zero used 3.41×10^23 FLOP and proves compute grows 10× a year.
stop_quoting.fact: 3.41e23 is OpenAI's 2018 estimate and counts the compute spent generating self-play games. Epoch's database now counts only direct network training: 6.5×10^20 FLOP for AlphaGo Zero ('Confident') and 3.4×10^20 for AlphaGo Master. Quote the basis with the number; neither figure supports a '10× a year' trend claim.
stop_quoting.source: Epoch AI Notable AI Models CSV (12 Nov 2026)

stop_quoting.claim: Google paid $500 million for DeepMind.
stop_quoting.fact: Terms were not disclosed. Reports ranged from $400 million (Re/code) to 'more than $500 million' (The Information).

stop_quoting.claim: XCON saved DEC $40 million a year.
stop_quoting.fact: Most accounts put R1/XCON's savings at about $25 million a year; $40 million was DEC's figure for XCON plus related expert systems.

stop_quoting.claim: Training frontier models is getting cheaper (AI Index 2026: −30%, ~$120M).
stop_quoting.fact: That figure comes from one secondary summary and could not be checked in the report (hai.stanford.edu unreachable). Epoch's trends page says frontier language-model training cost has risen ~3.5× a year since 2020, and its data put 2025 runs at $218M–$388M amortised (2023 USD) and Grok 4 at ~$490M nominal. Quote Epoch until the AI Index text is verified.
stop_quoting.source: Epoch AI trends page and CSV

stop_quoting.claim: The US produced 61 notable AI models in 2023.
stop_quoting.fact: 61 is the AI Index 2024 count; the AI Index 2025 restated 2023 as 70. Quote the edition. (2024: 40; 2025: 50 or 59 depending on the 2026 PDF vs web page.)

stop_quoting.claim: AI inference costs have fallen 280-fold.
stop_quoting.fact: Stanford's figure covers GPT-3.5-level capability from $20 (Nov 2022) to $0.07 (Oct 2024) per million tokens; it is not the price of frontier AI.

stop_quoting.claim: DeepSeek trained a frontier model for $5.6 million.
stop_quoting.fact: $5.58M was DeepSeek's stated GPU-rental cost for V3's final pre-training run only — excluding research, earlier runs, staff and hardware — and is not comparable with Epoch's ~$490M estimate for Grok 4.
stop_quoting.source: DeepSeek V3 technical report; Report AI

stop_quoting.claim: Claude Fable 5 was withdrawn within a week of launch (and is unavailable).
stop_quoting.fact: Anthropic suspended Fable 5 and Mythos 5 on 12 June 2026, three days after the 9 June launch, under a US export-control directive, and restored both on 1 July 2026 (Mythos 5 for a set of US organisations only). Fable 5.1 has been generally available since September 2026.
stop_quoting.source: Anthropic launch post with 12 Jun and 1 Jul updates
